a: Sunlight is made of all colours. Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths far more than long (red) ones — about 5× more — so blue light bounces around the whole sky before reaching your eyes.
tryit: At sunset, look for red and orange: the light travels through more air and the blue has been scattered away.

a: Nobody is 100% sure! The best-supported idea is that yawning cools the brain — a big stretch of the jaw pumps cooler blood upward. Yawns are also contagious, probably because of empathy.
tryit: Yawn dramatically in front of someone and count how many seconds until they yawn too.

a: Cats purr by vibrating muscles in their voice box 25–150 times a second. They purr when happy — but also when hurt or scared, which suggests purring soothes them and may even help bones heal.
tryit: Put your hand on a purring cat's throat and feel the buzz. Then hum and feel your own.

q: How do birds sleep without falling off branches?
a: Their toes have a tendon that automatically tightens when their legs bend. Sitting down = gripping. Some birds also sleep with one half of the brain awake.
tryit: Curl your fingers and press your wrist down: notice how your fingers tighten by themselves.

a: When water freezes, its molecules lock into a hexagon pattern that takes up MORE space than liquid water, so ice is about 9% less dense. Almost every other substance shrinks when it freezes.
tryit: Fill a plastic bottle to the brim, cap it, freeze it. What happens to the bottle?

q: Why do onions make us cry?
a: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases a gas that turns into a mild acid when it touches the water in your eyes. Your eyes make tears to wash it away.
tryit: Chill an onion in the fridge first and cut it near running water — fewer tears? Why?

q: How many bones are in your body?
a: Babies are born with about 300 bones; adults have 206. Many baby bones fuse together as you grow — like the skull, which starts as several plates.
tryit: Feel the bumps on the back of your hand: how many bones can you count in one finger?

a: Rain slowly dissolves minerals from rocks on land and rivers carry them to the sea. Water evaporates from the ocean but salt doesn't, so over millions of years it built up to about 3.5%.
tryit: Dissolve a spoon of salt in water, leave the dish in the sun for a few days, and see the salt come back.

a: Sort of. Fish don't have eyelids and don't have REM sleep like us, but many go into a resting state — slowing down, hovering in place, some even ‘bury’ in sand. Sharks that must keep moving rest half their brain at a time.
tryit: Watch a fish tank at night with a dim light. Do the fish move differently?

q: Why do leaves change colour in autumn?
a: Leaves are always yellow and orange underneath — the green chlorophyll just hides it. When days shorten, trees stop making chlorophyll and the hidden colours show. Reds are made fresh from sugars trapped in the leaf.
tryit: Collect leaves of one tree over three weeks and tape them in order.

a: Tiny muscles at the base of each hair pull it upright when you're cold or scared. On furry animals this traps warm air or makes them look bigger. We kept the reflex, just not the fur.
tryit: Watch a cat's tail when a dog appears — that's goosebumps doing their real job.

q: How does a plane stay up?
a: Wings are shaped so air moving over the top speeds up and pushes down less than the air underneath pushes up — plus the wing deflects air downward, and the air pushes the wing up in return. Engines provide the speed.
tryit: Hold a strip of paper under your bottom lip and blow across the top. It lifts!

a: Seeing a yawn activates the same brain areas you'd use to yawn yourself — mirror neurons. Contagious yawning appears around age 4–5 and is stronger between friends and family.
tryit: Count contagious yawns at dinner. Who's most ‘catchy’?

q: Why does the Moon change shape?
a: The Moon doesn't change — how much of its sunlit half we can see does, as it circles Earth every 29.5 days. A full Moon is when Earth is between Sun and Moon.
tryit: Shine a torch on a ball in a dark room and walk around it. Watch the ‘phases’.

a: Two jobs: they stop sweat and rain running into your eyes, and they're a huge part of how faces communicate. People recognise faces with no eyes better than faces with no eyebrows!
tryit: Cover your eyebrows with your fingers and make faces in a mirror. Harder to read?

a: Bees drink flower nectar into a special stomach, pass it mouth-to-mouth adding enzymes, spit it into wax cells and fan it with their wings until most water evaporates. One jar = about 2 million flower visits.
tryit: Watch a bee on a flower for one minute. Count the flowers it visits.

a: Your brain predicts what your own hands will do and cancels the surprise. Tickling only works when the touch is unexpected — that's why someone else can do it.
tryit: Try tickling your own foot. Now let someone else. Notice the difference.

a: Starlight is a tiny point that gets bent by moving layers of air in our atmosphere. Planets are close enough to look like tiny discs, so they usually don't twinkle.
tryit: Find the steadiest bright ‘star’ in the sky — it's probably a planet.

a: Scientists think dreams help sort memories, practise emotions and solve problems. Everyone dreams every night — about 2 hours — but we forget most of them within minutes.
tryit: Keep a notebook by the bed and write down one dream before you get up.

a: Their skin has tiny crystals they can stretch or squeeze, changing which colours reflect. They mostly change for mood and temperature — not to match the background!
tryit: Mix food colouring in water: how does adding more change the shade?

a: Yeast are tiny living fungi. They eat sugars in the flour and burp out carbon dioxide gas, which puffs up thousands of bubbles in the stretchy dough.
tryit: Mix warm water, a spoon of sugar and yeast in a bottle. Put a balloon on top and wait 30 minutes.

a: Blood carries oxygen using a protein called haemoglobin, which contains iron. Iron bound to oxygen looks bright red — like rust. Some crabs have blue blood using copper instead!
tryit: Look at the veins in your wrist: they look blue because of how skin filters light, but the blood inside is red.

a: A sudden spasm of your diaphragm (the breathing muscle) pulls in air, then your vocal cords snap shut — ‘hic’. Nobody knows exactly why; one idea is it's leftover from how tadpoles breathe.
tryit: Try the spoon-of-sugar trick or breathing into a paper bag. Which works for you?

a: Roots pull in water, and it climbs up tiny tubes in the stem like a straw. Water molecules stick together, so as leaves lose water into the air, they pull more water up behind — even to the top of a 100 m tree.
tryit: Put a white flower or celery in coloured water overnight. Watch where the colour goes.

a: Gravity pulls everything toward the centre equally from all directions. Anything big enough — over about 500 km across — gets squashed into a ball. Small asteroids stay lumpy.
tryit: Squeeze play-dough evenly from all sides. What shape does it become?

a: During sleep your brain files memories, clears out waste chemicals, and your body repairs itself and grows. Kids grow the most during deep sleep!
tryit: Tonight, note how you feel after 9+ hours vs a short night. Which is better?

a: The Sun heats some places more than others. Warm air rises, cooler air rushes in to fill the gap — that rush is wind. Big differences make big winds.
tryit: Hold a tissue over a warm radiator. Which way does it move?

q: Why do our fingers wrinkle in the bath?
a: Nerves make blood vessels under the skin shrink, pulling the skin into ridges — like tyre treads. Scientists showed wrinkled fingers grip wet things better!
tryit: Soak one hand for 10 minutes, then pick up wet marbles with each hand. Which is faster?

q: Why do dogs wag their tails?
a: It's language. Wag to the right often means happy; to the left, unsure; fast and high can be excited or alert; low and slow can be nervous. Dogs read each other's wags.
tryit: Watch a dog meet someone. Which way does the tail swing?

a: Sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back and bends again on the way out — splitting into colours. You need the Sun behind you and rain in front.
tryit: With the Sun behind you, spray a hose in a fine mist and look for your own rainbow.

a: Laughter is social glue — we laugh 30× more with others than alone. It signals ‘this is play, we're safe’, releases feel-good chemicals and even reduces pain slightly.
tryit: Try to make someone laugh without words. What worked?

a: The soap film pulls itself as tight as possible, and a sphere is the shape with the least surface for the air inside. Nature is lazy in the best way.
tryit: Blow a bubble through a square wand. Is the bubble square?

a: Each kernel has a drop of water inside a hard shell. Heat turns it to steam, pressure builds to about 9 atmospheres, then the shell bursts and the starch puffs out and sets.
tryit: Count the ‘old maids’ (unpopped kernels) in a bowl. Why might they not pop?

a: Sound is air wobbling. It shakes your eardrum, which shakes three tiny bones, which shake fluid in a snail-shaped tube lined with hairs. Different hairs fire for different pitches.
tryit: Stretch plastic wrap over a bowl, sprinkle rice, and shout at it.

a: Deep underground, rock is so hot it melts into magma. It's lighter than the rock around it, so it rises. Gas bubbles build pressure — like a shaken soda — until it bursts through.
tryit: Vinegar + baking soda + a squirt of dish soap in a bottle = a safe kitchen eruption.

a: Snow is made of clear ice crystals, but each one bounces light in all directions. Millions of crystals reflect all colours together — and all colours mixed is white.
tryit: Look closely at a single snowflake on a dark sleeve — it's clear, not white!

q: How do birds know where to migrate?
a: They use the Sun, the stars, landmarks — and a built-in compass that senses Earth's magnetic field. Young birds learn the route from older ones.
tryit: Look up which birds leave your area in autumn and where they're heading.

a: Tiny cells called platelets rush to the cut and stick together, then a protein called fibrin weaves a net that dries into a scab — a natural bandage while new skin grows underneath.
tryit: Don't pick it! Check how many days a small scab takes to fall off by itself.

q: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
a: They're the same temperature! Metal pulls heat out of your hand much faster, so your skin senses ‘cold’. Wood is a poor conductor, so it feels warmer.
tryit: Touch a metal spoon and a wooden spoon from the same drawer. Then check with a thermometer.

q: Why do we have two eyes?
a: Each eye sees a slightly different picture. Your brain compares them to work out depth — how far things are. Close one eye and try to touch fingertips at arm's length!
tryit: Do the fingertip test with one eye, then two. Which is easier?

a: Light travels 300,000 km every second. It takes 8 minutes from the Sun, 4 years from the next star, and 2.5 million years from the nearest big galaxy. The observable universe is 93 billion light-years across.
tryit: Count to 8 slowly: that's how ‘old’ the sunlight on your face is.

a: Baby teeth are placeholders. Adult teeth grow underneath and dissolve the baby roots, so the tooth gets wobbly and falls out. You get 20 baby teeth and 32 adult ones.
tryit: Look at a wobbly tooth in a mirror — can you see the new one waiting?
